blocks.text: Target modules specify exactly which weight matrices inside a model LoRA actually inserts its low rank update pairs into, a choice that directly shapes both how many trainable parameters a LoRA setup uses and how much of the model behavior it can actually influence.
This topic covers the common target module choices, the tradeoffs between targeting fewer versus more of them, and how to identify the correct module names for a specific model architecture.
1. What Target Modules Are

blocks.alt: A transformer layer contains many weight matrices, and target modules are the chosen subset to target

blocks.text: A single transformer layer, covered in the Foundation Models module, contains several distinct weight matrices, attention projections, feed-forward layers, and more, and target modules specify precisely which of those matrices LoRA actually attaches its low rank updates to, rather than every matrix in the model.
2. Common Target Modules in a Transformer

blocks.alt: Query, key, and value projections are common attention targets

blocks.text: The most commonly targeted modules are the query, key, and value projection matrices inside the attention mechanism, covered in the Foundation Models module, since these matrices heavily influence how the model relates different parts of the input to each other, making them a natural, high leverage place to apply a learned adjustment.

code.content:
# A common target module configuration, conceptually
target_modules = ["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj"]

blocks.text: 3. Attention Projections as the Usual Default

For many fine-tuning tasks, targeting only the attention projection matrices provides a strong, efficient starting point, since these matrices govern much of the model contextual understanding, exactly where a fine-tuning task like adjusting how the model weighs different pieces of context can have an outsized effect.
4. Extending to Feed-Forward Layers

blocks.alt: Attention projections only is compared against attention plus feed-forward layers

blocks.text: Some setups also target the feed-forward layers within each transformer block, in addition to the attention projections, giving the LoRA update more surface area to influence model behavior, at the cost of additional trainable parameters.
5. Fewer Target Modules, Fewer Parameters

blocks.alt: Fewer target modules produce fewer parameters overall

blocks.text: Every additional targeted module adds its own pair of low rank matrices and therefore its own share of trainable parameters, so targeting only a few carefully chosen modules, rather than every matrix in the model, keeps the total parameter count, and the resulting training and memory cost, low.
6. More Target Modules, More Expressiveness

blocks.alt: More target modules provide more expressiveness

blocks.text: Targeting more modules gives the LoRA update more places in the network to actually influence, which can meaningfully improve results on tasks that need a broader behavioral shift than the attention projections alone can capture well.

blocks.text: 7. How to Choose Target Modules for a Task

blocks.alt: The task type informs the target module choice

blocks.text: A reasonable starting approach targets attention projections only, since this covers many common fine-tuning tasks well, and expands to include feed-forward layers specifically if evaluation results suggest the model is not learning the target behavior strongly enough with the narrower set.

blocks.title: This mirrors the rank tuning approach from the earlier topic
blocks.content: Just as rank benefits from experimental tuning rather than a single guessed value, target module choice is worth testing empirically against a specific task rather than assuming one configuration fits every situation.

blocks.text: 8. Inspecting a Model to Find Valid Target Module Names

blocks.alt: Inspecting a model architecture reveals the valid layer names to target

blocks.text: The exact names used for target modules, q_proj, k_proj, or entirely different naming, depend on the specific model architecture and implementation, making it necessary to inspect the model layer names directly before configuring a LoRA setup for a new base model.
9. A Practical Default Recommendation

For most new fine-tuning projects, starting with query and value projections, sometimes just those two rather than all three attention matrices, is a widely used, well tested default that many practitioners reach for before considering whether a broader set of target modules is genuinely needed for the specific task at hand.
Worked Example

A team fine-tunes a model targeting only the query and value attention projections, following the common default, and finds their tone adjustment task, a fairly narrow behavioral shift, performs well with this minimal target module set.

A separate team teaching a model a more substantial new skill finds the same narrow target module set underperforms, and after expanding to also include the feed-forward layers, sees a clear improvement, confirming their more demanding task genuinely benefited from the broader targeting.
Common Mistakes

items: Guessing target module names without inspecting the actual model architecture first, leading to a configuration error
Targeting every possible weight matrix by default, unnecessarily inflating parameter count for a task that did not need it
Sticking with a minimal target module set even after evaluation clearly shows it is insufficient for the task
Assuming target module names are standardized across every model architecture, when they often differ

blocks.text: Practice

If you have access to any pretrained model, print out its named modules and identify which layer names correspond to the attention query, key, and value projections, confirming you could correctly configure a target module list for that specific model.
Key Takeaway

Target modules determine exactly which weight matrices a LoRA update actually attaches to, with attention projections serving as a strong, widely used default that keeps parameter count low, and expanding to include feed-forward layers when a task genuinely needs the additional expressiveness that broader targeting provides.
